*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and by my God.”

*Study note:* *I can jump over a wall*. The psalmist uses hyperbole to emphasize his God-given military superiority.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[As for] the God, his way is blameless.” The term הָאֵל (haʾel, “the God”) stands as a nominative (or genitive) absolute in apposition to the resumptive pronominal suffix on “way.” The prefixed article emphasizes his distinctiveness as the one true God (cf. {{Deuteronomy 33:26|Deut 33:26}}). God’s “way” in this context refers to his protective and salvific acts in fulfillment of his promise (see also {{Deuteronomy 32:4|Deut 32:4}}; {{Psalm 67:2|Pss 67:2}}; {{Psalm 77:13|77:13}} [note vv. {{Psalm 77:11|11-12}}, {{Psalm 77:14|14}}]; {{Psalm 103:7|103:7}}; {{Psalm 138:5|138:5}}; {{Psalm 145:17|145:17}}).

*Study note:* *The* Lord’*s promise*. In the ancient Near East kings would typically seek and receive oracles from their god(s) prior to battle. For examples, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 241-42.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the word of the Lord is purified.” The Lord’s “word” probably refers here to his oracle(s) of victory delivered to the psalmist before the battle(s) described in the following context. See also {{Psalm 12:5|Pss 12:5-7}} and {{Psalm 138:2|138:2-3}}. David frequently received such oracles before going into battle (see {{1 Samuel 23:2|1 Sam 23:2}}, {{1 Samuel 23:4|4-5}}, {{1 Samuel 23:10|10-12}}; {{1 Samuel 30:8|30:8}}; {{2 Samuel 5:19|2 Sam 5:19}}). The Lord’s word of promise is absolutely reliable; it is compared to metal that has been refined in fire and cleansed of impurities. See {{Psalm 12:6|Ps 12:6}}.

*Study note:* *Take shelter*. See the note on the word “shelter” in v. {{Psalm 18:2|2}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rocky cliff,” which is a metaphor of divine protection. See v. {{Psalm 18:2|2}}, where the Hebrew term צוּר (tsur) is translated “rocky summit.”

*Translator's note:* The rhetorical questions anticipate the answer, “No one.” In this way the psalmist indicates that the Lord is the only true God and reliable source of protection. See also {{Deuteronomy 32:39|Deut 32:39}}, where the Lord affirms that he is the only true God. Note as well the emphasis on his role as protector (*Heb* “rocky cliff,” צוּר, tsur) in {{Deuteronomy 32:4|Deut 32:4}}, {{Deuteronomy 32:15|15}}, {{Deuteronomy 32:17|17-18}}, {{Deuteronomy 32:30|30}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God.” The prefixed article emphasizes the Lord’s distinctiveness as the one true God (cf. {{Deuteronomy 33:26|Deut 33:26}}). See v. {{Psalm 18:30|30}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “is the one who clothes.” For similar language see {{1 Samuel 2:4|1 Sam 2:4}}; {{Psalm 65:6|Pss 65:6}}; {{Psalm 93:1|93:1}}. The psalmist employs a generalizing hymnic style in vv. {{Psalm 18:32|32-34}}; he uses participles in vv. {{Psalm 18:32|32a}}, {{Psalm 18:33|33a}}, and {{Psalm 18:34|34a}} to describe what God characteristically does on his behalf.

*Translator's note:* {{2 Samuel 22:33|2 Sam 22:33}} reads, “the God is my strong refuge.”

*Study note:* *Gives me strength*. As the following context makes clear, this refers to physical and emotional strength for battle (see especially v. {{Psalm 18:39|39}}).

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) consecutive here carries along the generalizing force of the preceding participle.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he made my path smooth.” The Hebrew term תָּמִים (tamim, “smooth”) usually carries a moral or ethical connotation, “blameless, innocent.” However, in {{Psalm 18:33|Ps 18:33}} it refers to a pathway free of obstacles. The reality underlying the metaphor is the psalmist’s ability to charge into battle without tripping (see vv. {{Psalm 18:33|33}}, {{Psalm 18:36|36}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the one who] makes my feet like [those of ] a deer.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and on my high places he makes me walk.” The imperfect verbal form emphasizes God’s characteristic provision. The psalmist compares his agility in battle to the ability of a deer to negotiate rugged, high terrain without falling or being injured.

*Study note:* Habakkuk uses similar language to describe his faith during difficult times. See {{Habakkuk 3:19|Hab 3:19}}.

*Study note:* *He trains my hands*. The psalmist attributes his skill with weapons to divine enablement. Egyptian reliefs picture gods teaching the king how to shoot a bow. See O. Keel, *The Symbolism of the Biblical World*, 265.

*Study note:* The *strongest bow* (*Heb* “bow of bronze”) probably refers to a bow laminated with bronze strips, or to a purely ceremonial or decorative bow made entirely from bronze. In the latter case the language is hyperbolic, for such a weapon would not be functional in battle.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and a bow of bronze is bent by my arms”; or “my arms bend a bow of bronze.” The verb נָחַת (nakhat) apparently means “pull back, bend” here (see *HALOT* 692 s.v. נחת). The third feminine singular verbal form appears to agree with the feminine singular noun קֶשֶׁת (qeshet, “bow”). In this case the verb must be taken as Niphal (passive). However, it is possible that “my arms” is the subject of the verb and “bow” the object. In this case the verb is Piel (active). For other examples of a feminine singular verb being construed with a plural noun, see GKC 464 §145.*k*.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you give to me the shield of your deliverance.”

*Study note:* *You give me your protective shield*. Ancient Near Eastern literature often refers to a god giving a king special weapons. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 260-61.

*Text-critical note:* {{2 Samuel 22:36|2 Sam 22:36}} omits this line, perhaps due to homoioarcton. A scribe’s eye may have jumped from the vav (ו) prefixed to “your right hand” to the vav prefixed to the following “and your answer,” causing the copyist to omit by accident the intervening words (“your right hand supports me and”).

*Translator's note:* The MT of {{Psalm 18:35|Ps 18:35}} appears to read, “your condescension,” apparently referring to God’s willingness to intervene (cf. NIV84 “you stoop down”). However, the noun עֲנָוָה (ʿanavah) elsewhere means “humility” and is used only here of God. The form עַנְוַתְךָ (ʿanvatekha) may be a fully written form of the suffixed infinitive construct of עָנָה (ʿanah, “to answer”; a defectively written form of the infinitive appears in {{2 Samuel 22:36|2 Sam 22:36}}). In this case the psalmist refers to God’s willingness to answer his prayer; one might translate, “your favorable response” (cf. NIV11 “your help”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “makes me great.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you make wide my step under me.” “Step” probably refers metonymically to the path upon which the psalmist walks. Another option is to translate, “you widen my stride.” This would suggest that God gives the psalmist the capacity to run quickly.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lower legs.” On the meaning of the Hebrew noun, which occurs only here, see H. R. Cohen, *Biblical Hapax Legomena* (SBLDS), 112. A cognate Akkadian noun means “lower leg.”

*Translator's note:* Or “smash them.” {{2 Samuel 22:39|2 Sam 22:39}} reads, “and I wiped them out and smashed them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “until they are unable to rise.” {{2 Samuel 22:39|2 Sam 22:39}} reads, “until they do not rise.”

*Study note:* *They fall at my feet*. For ancient Near Eastern parallels, see O. Keel, *The Symbolism of the Biblical World*, 294-97.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “clothed me.” See v. {{Psalm 18:32|32}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you make those who rise against me kneel beneath me.”

*Study note:* *My foes kneel before me*. For ancient Near Eastern parallels, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 268.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [as for] my enemies, you give to me [the] back [or “neck”].” The idiom “give [the] back” means “to cause [one] to turn the back and run away.” Cf. {{Exodus 23:27|Exod 23:27}}.

*Study note:* *Those who hate me*. See v. {{Psalm 18:17|17}}, where it is the Lord who delivered the psalmist from those who hated him.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but there is no deliverer.”

*Study note:* *They cry out*. This reference to the psalmist’s enemies crying out for help to the Lord suggests that the psalmist refers here to enemies within the covenant community, rather than foreigners. However, the militaristic context suggests foreign enemies are in view. Ancient Near Eastern literature indicates that defeated enemies would sometimes cry out for mercy to the god(s) of their conqueror. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 271.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the Lord.” The words “they cry out” are supplied in the translation because they are understood by ellipsis (see the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I pulverize them like dust upon the face of the wind.” The phrase “upon the face of” here means “before.” {{2 Samuel 22:43|2 Sam 22:43}} reads, “like dust of the earth.”

*Text-critical note:* {{Psalm 18:42|Ps 18:42}} reads, “I empty them out” (Hiphil of ריק), while {{2 Samuel 22:43|2 Sam 22:43}} reads, “I crush them, I stomp on them” (juxtaposing the synonyms דקק and רקע). It is likely that the latter is a conflation of variants. One, but not both, of the verbs in {{2 Samuel 22:43|2 Sam 22:43}} is probably original; “empty out” does not form as good a parallel with “grind, pulverize” in the parallel line.

*Translator's note:* Or “mud.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the strivings of a people.” In this context the Hebrew term רִיב (riv, “striving”) probably has a militaristic sense (as in {{Judges 12:2|Judg 12:2}}; {{Isaiah 41:11|Isa 41:11}}), and עָם (ʿam, “people”) probably refers more specifically to an army (for other examples, see the verses listed in BDB 766 s.v. I עַם, עָם 2.d). Some understand the phrase as referring to attacks by the psalmist’s own countrymen, the “nation” being Israel. However, foreign enemies appear to be in view; note the reference to “nations” in the following line.

*Translator's note:* {{2 Samuel 22:44|2 Sam 22:44}} reads, “you keep me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a people whom I did not know serve me.” In this context “know” (יָדַע, yadaʿ) probably refers to formal recognition by treaty. People who were once not under the psalmist’s authority now willingly submit to his rulership to avoid being conquered militarily (see vv. {{Psalm 18:44|44-45}}). The language may recall the events recorded in {{2 Samuel 8:9|2 Sam 8:9-10}} and {{2 Samuel 10:19|10:19}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at a report of an ear they submit to me.” The report of the psalmist’s exploits is so impressive that those who hear it submit to his rulership without putting up a fight.

*Translator's note:* For the meaning “be weak, powerless” for כָּחַשׁ (kakhash), see {{Psalm 109:24|Ps 109:24}}. The next line (see v. {{Psalm 18:45|45a}}), in which “foreigners” are also mentioned, favors this interpretation. Another option is to translate “cower in fear” (see {{Deuteronomy 33:29|Deut 33:29}}; {{Psalm 66:3|Pss 66:3}}; {{Psalm 81:15|81:15}}; cf. NIV84 “cringe”; NIV11 “cower”; NRSV “came cringing”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wither, wear out.”

*Translator's note:* The meaning of חָרַג (kharag, “shake”) is established on the basis of cognates in Arabic and Aramaic. {{2 Samuel 22:46|2 Sam 22:46}} reads חָגַר (khagar), which might mean here, “[they] come limping” (on the basis of a cognate in postbiblical Hebrew). The normal meaning for חָגַר (“gird”) makes little sense here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their prisons.” The besieged cities of the foreigners are compared to prisons.

*Translator's note:* Elsewhere the construction חַי־יְהוָה (khay yehvah) is used exclusively as an oath formula, “as surely as the Lord lives,” but this is not the case here, for no oath follows. Here the statement is an affirmation of the Lord’s active presence and intervention. In contrast to pagan deities, he demonstrates he is the living God by rescuing and empowering the psalmist.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my rocky cliff,” which is a metaphor for protection. See similar phrases in vv. {{Psalm 18:2|2}}, {{Psalm 18:31|31}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “blessed [i.e., praised] be.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God of my deliverance.” {{2 Samuel 22:48|2 Sam 22:48}} reads, “the God of the rocky cliff of my deliverance.”

*Translator's note:* The words “as king” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Elsewhere in the psalms the verb רוּם (rum, “be exalted”), when used of God, refers to his exalted position as king ({{Psalm 99:2|Pss 99:2}}; {{Psalm 113:4|113:4}}; {{Psalm 138:6|138:6}}) and/or his self-revelation as king through his mighty deeds of deliverance ({{Psalm 21:13|Pss 21:13}}; {{Psalm 46:10|46:10}}; {{Psalm 57:5|57:5}}, {{Psalm 57:11|11}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God.” See v. {{Psalm 18:32|32}}.

*Study note:* *Completely vindicates me*. In the ancient Near East military victory was sometimes viewed as a sign that one’s God had judged in favor of the victor, avenging and/or vindicating him. See, for example, {{Judges 11:27|Judg 11:27}}, {{Judges 11:32|32-33}}, {{Judges 11:36|36}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “is the one who grants vengeance to me.” The plural form of the noun indicates degree here, suggesting complete vengeance or vindication.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he subdues nations beneath me.” On the meaning of the verb דָּבַר (davar, “subdue,” a homonym of דָּבַר, davar, “speak”), see *HALOT* 209-10 s.v. I דבר. See also {{Psalm 47:3|Ps 47:3}} and 2 Chr 22:10. {{2 Samuel 22:48|2 Sam 22:48}} reads “and [is the one who] brings down nations beneath me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the one who] delivers me.” {{2 Samuel 22:49|2 Sam 22:49}} reads “and [the one who] brings me out.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lifts me up.” In light of the preceding and following references to deliverance, the verb רום probably here refers to being rescued from danger (see {{Psalm 9:13|Ps 9:13}}). However, it could mean “exalt, elevate” here, indicating that the Lord has given the psalmist victory over his enemies and forced them to acknowledge the psalmist’s superiority (cf. NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from those who rise against me.”

*Study note:* *I will give you thanks before the nations*. This probably alludes to the fact that the psalmist will praise the Lord in the presence of the defeated nations when they, as his subjects, bring their tribute payments. Ideally the Davidic king was to testify to the nations of God’s greatness. See J. H. Eaton, *Kingship and the Psalms* (SBT), 182-85.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to your name.” God’s “name” refers metonymically to his divine characteristics as suggested by his name, in this case “Lord,” the primary name of Israel’s covenant God which suggests his active presence with his people (see {{Exodus 3:12|Exod 3:12-15}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “the one who.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “magnifies the victories of his king.” “His king” refers to the psalmist, the Davidic king whom God has chosen to rule Israel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the one who] does loyalty.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his anointed [one],” i.e., the psalmist/Davidic king. See {{Psalm 2:2|Ps 2:2}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “offspring”; *Heb* “seed.”

*Study note:* If *David* is the author of the psalm (see the superscription), then he here anticipates that God will continue to demonstrate loyalty to his descendants who succeed him. If the author is a later Davidic king, then he views the divine favor he has experienced as the outworking of God’s faithful promises to David his ancestor.

*Study note:* *Psalm 19*. The psalmist praises God for his self-revelation in the heavens and in the Mosaic law. The psalmist concludes with a prayer, asking the Lord to keep him from sinning and to approve of his thoughts and words.

*Study note:* God’s *glory* refers here to his royal majesty and power.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the work of his hands the sky declares.” The participles emphasize the ongoing testimony of the heavens/sky.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it gushes forth a word.” The “sky” (see v. {{Psalm 19:1|1b}}) is the subject of the verb. Though not literally speaking (see v. {{Psalm 19:3|3}}), it clearly reveals God’s royal majesty. The sun’s splendor and its movement across the sky is in view (see vv. {{Psalm 19:4|4-6}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it [i.e., the sky] declares knowledge,” i.e., knowledge about God’s royal majesty and power (see v. {{Psalm 19:1|1}}). This apparently refers to the splendor and movements of the stars. The imperfect verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 19:2|2}}, like the participles in the preceding verse, combine with the temporal phrases (“day after day” and “night after night”) to emphasize the ongoing testimony of the sky.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their.” The antecedent of the plural pronoun is “heavens” (v. {{Psalm 19:1|1}}).

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads, “their measuring line” (קוּם, qum). The noun קַו (qav, “measuring line”) makes no sense in this context. The reading קוֹלָם (qolam, “their voice”) which is supported by the LXX, is preferable.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “goes out,” or “proceeds forth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their” (see the note on the word “its” in v. {{Psalm 19:3|3}}).

*Translator's note:* The verb is supplied in the translation. The Hebrew text has no verb; יָצָא (yatsaʾ, “goes out”) is understood by ellipsis.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the end of the world.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in them” (i.e., the heavens).

*Study note:* *He has pitched a tent for the sun*. The personified sun emerges from this “tent” in order to make its daytime journey across the sky. So the “tent” must refer metaphorically to the place where the sun goes to rest during the night.

*Translator's note:* The participle expresses the repeated or regular nature of the action.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun חֻפָּה (khufah, “chamber”) occurs elsewhere only in {{Isaiah 4:5|Isa 4:5}} and Joel 2:16 (where it refers to the bedroom of a bride and groom).

*Study note:* *Like a bridegroom*. The metaphor likens the sun to a bridegroom who rejoices on his wedding night.

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form draws attention to the regularity of the action.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[on] a path.”

*Study note:* *Like a strong man*. The metaphorical language reflects the brilliance of the sunrise, which attests to the sun’s vigor.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the end of the heavens [is] its going forth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and its circuit [is] to their ends.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “is hidden from.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[it] restores life.” Elsewhere the Hiphil of שׁוּב (shuv, “return”) when used with נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “life”) as object, means to “rescue or preserve one’s life” ({{Job 33:30|Job 33:30}}; {{Psalm 35:17|Ps 35:17}}) or to “revive one’s strength” (emotionally or physically; cf. {{Ruth 4:15|Ruth 4:15}}; Lam 1:11, 16, 19). Here the point seems to be that the law preserves the life of the one who studies it by making known God’s will. Those who know God’s will know how to please him and can avoid offending him. See v. {{Psalm 19:11|11a}}.

*Translator's note:* Traditionally, “the testimony of the Lord.” The noun עֵדוּת (ʿedut) refers here to the demands of God’s covenant law.

*Translator's note:* God’s covenant contains a clear, reliable witness to his moral character and demands.

*Translator's note:* Or “the [morally] naive,” that is, the one who is young and still in the process of learning right from wrong and distinguishing wisdom from folly.

*Translator's note:* Or “just.” Perhaps the idea is that they impart a knowledge of what is just and right.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[they] make happy [the] heart.” Perhaps the point is that they bring a sense of joyful satisfaction to the one who knows and keeps them, for those who obey God’s law are richly rewarded. See v. {{Psalm 19:11|11b}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “command.” The singular here refers to the law as a whole.

*Translator's note:* Because they reflect God’s character, his commands provide a code of moral and ethical purity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* [they] enlighten [the] eyes.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fear of the Lord is clean.” The phrase “fear of the Lord” probably refers here to the law, which teaches one how to demonstrate proper reverence for the Lord. See {{Psalm 111:10|Ps 111:10}} for another possible use of the phrase in this sense.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[it] stands permanently.”

*Study note:* *Trustworthy and absolutely just*. The Lord’s commands accurately reflect God’s moral will for his people and are an expression of his just character.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “more desirable.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “are sweeter.” God’s law is “sweet’ in the sense that, when obeyed, it brings a great reward (see v. {{Psalm 19:11|11b}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “moreover your servant is warned by them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the keeping of them [there is] a great reward.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Errors who can discern?” This rhetorical question makes the point that perfect moral discernment is impossible to achieve. Consequently it is inevitable that even those with good intentions will sin on occasion.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “declare me innocent from hidden [things],” i.e., sins. In this context (see the preceding line) “hidden” sins are not sins committed in secret, but sins which are not recognized as such by the psalmist.

*Translator's note:* Or “presumptuous sins.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let them not rule over me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “great.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may the words of my mouth and the thought of my heart be acceptable before you.” The prefixed verbal form at the beginning of the verse is understood as a jussive of prayer. Another option is to translate the form as an imperfect continuing the thought of v. {{Psalm 19:14|14b}}: “[Then] the words of my mouth and the thought of my heart will be acceptable before you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my rocky cliff,” which is a metaphor for protection; thus the translation “sheltering rock.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the one who redeems me.” The metaphor casts the Lord in the role of a leader who protects members of his extended family in times of need and crisis.

*Study note:* *Psalm 20*. The people pray for the king’s success in battle. When the king declares his assurance that the Lord will answer the people’s prayer, they affirm their confidence in God’s enablement.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal forms here and in vv. {{Psalm 20:1|1b-5}} are interpreted as jussives of prayer (cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV). Another option is to understand them as imperfects, “the Lord will answer,” etc. In this case the people declare their confidence that the Lord will intervene on behalf of the king and extend to him his favor.

*Study note:* *May the* Lord *answer you*. The people address the king as they pray to the Lord.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in a day of trouble.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the name of the God of Jacob.” God’s “name” refers metonymically to his very person and to the divine characteristics suggested by his name, in this case “God of Jacob,” which highlights his relationship to Israel.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “from [the] temple.” The third masculine singular pronominal suffix (וֹ, holem vav) has probably been accidentally omitted by haplography. Note that the following word begins with a prefixed vav (ו). See P. C. Craigie, *{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* (WBC), 184.

*Translator's note:* Or “remember.” For other examples of the verb זָכַר (zakhar) carrying the nuance “take notice of,” see {{Psalm 8:4|Pss 8:4}} and {{Psalm 9:12|9:12}}.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “consider as fat.” The verbal form should probably be emended to יְדַשְּׁנֶהָ (yedasheneha), the final he (ה) being understood as a third feminine singular pronominal suffix referring back to the feminine noun “burnt sacrifice.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may he give to you according to your heart.” This probably refers to the king’s prayer for protection and victory in battle. See vv. {{Psalm 20:5|5-6}}.

*Study note:* *May he bring all your plans to pass*. This probably refers to the king’s strategy for battle.

*Study note:* *Your victory*. Here the king is addressed (see v. {{Psalm 20:1|1}}).

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew verb דָּגַל (dagal) occurs only here in the Qal. If accepted as original, it may carry the nuance “raise a banner,” but it is preferable to emend the form to נָגִיל (nagil, “we will rejoice”) which provides better parallelism with “shout for joy” and fits well with the prepositional phrase “in the name of our God” (see {{Psalm 89:16|Ps 89:16}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “know.”

*Study note:* *Now I am sure*. The speaker is not identified. It is likely that the king, referring to himself in the third person (note “his chosen king”), responds to the people’s prayer. Perhaps his confidence is due to the reception of a divine oracle of salvation.

*Translator's note:* The perfect verbal form is probably used rhetorically to state that the deliverance is as good as done. In this way the speaker emphasizes the certainty of the deliverance. Another option is to take the statement as generalizing; the psalmist affirms that the Lord typically delivers the king.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his anointed one.” This title refers to the Davidic king. See {{Psalm 2:2|Pss 2:2}} and {{Psalm 18:50|18:50}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will answer him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from his holy heavens.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with mighty acts of deliverance of his right hand.” The Lord’s “right hand” here symbolizes his power to protect and deliver (see {{Psalm 17:7|Ps 17:7}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “these in chariots and these in horses.” No verb appears; the verb “invoke” is to be supplied from the following line. The convention of backward ellipsis can apply to the final word of the 2nd line, as in this verse. In this case the idea would be that some “invoke” (i.e., trust in) their military might for victory (cf. NEB “boast”; NIV “trust”; NRSV “take pride”). Verse {{Psalm 20:8|8}} suggests that the “some/others” mentioned here are the nation’s enemies.

*Translator's note:* The grammatical construction (conjunction + pronominal subject) highlights the contrast between God’s faithful people and the others mentioned in the previous line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “we invoke the name of.” The Hiphil of זָכַר (zakhar), when combined with the phrase “in the name,” means “to invoke” (see {{Joshua 23:7|Josh 23:7}}; {{Isaiah 48:1|Isa 48:1}}; {{Amos 6:10|Amos 6:10}}). By invoking the Lord’s name in prayer, the people demonstrate their trust in him.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX translates the verb as μεγαλυνθησόμεθα (megalunthēsometha) “we will boast.” This may reflect another verb, the Hiphil of גָּבַר (gavar), and depends on two letter confusions, ג (gimel) for ז (zayin) and ב (bet) for כ (kaf).

*Translator's note:* Or “stumble and fall down.”

*Translator's note:* The grammatical construction (conjunction + pronominal subject) highlights the contrast between God’s victorious people and the defeated enemies mentioned in the previous line. The perfect verbal forms either generalize or, more likely, state rhetorically the people’s confidence as they face the approaching battle. They describe the demise of the enemy as being as good as done.

*Translator's note:* Or “rise up and remain upright.” On the meaning of the Hitpolel of עוּד (ʿud), see *HALOT* 795 s.v. I עוד. The verbal forms (a perfect followed by a prefixed form with vav [ו] consecutive) either generalize or, more likely, state rhetorically the people’s confidence as they face the approaching battle.

*Text-critical note:* This translation assumes an emendation of the verbal form הוֹשִׁיעָה (hoshiʿah). As it stands, the form is an imperative. In this case the people return to the petitionary mood with which the psalm begins (“O Lord, deliver”). But the immediate context is one of confidence (vv. {{Psalm 20:6|6-8}}), not petition (vv. {{Psalm 20:1|1-5}}). If one takes the final he on the verb “deliver” as dittographic (note the initial he (ה) on the following phrase, “the king”), one can repoint the verbal form as a perfect and understand it as expressing the people’s confidence, “the Lord will deliver the king” (see v. {{Psalm 20:6|6}}). The Hebrew scribal tradition takes “the king” with the following line, in which case it would be best interpreted as a divine title, “may the King answer us” or “the king will answer us” (see {{Psalm 98:6|Pss 98:6}}; {{Psalm 145:1|145:1}}). However, the poetic parallelism is better balanced if “the king” is taken with the first line. In this case the referent is the Davidic king, who is earlier called the Lord’s “anointed one” (cf. note on “chosen king” in v. {{Psalm 20:6|6}}; see {{Psalm 21:7|Pss 21:7}}; {{Psalm 45:5|45:5}}, {{Psalm 45:11|11}}; {{Psalm 63:11|63:11}}).

*Translator's note:* If the imperative is retained in the preceding line, then the prefixed verbal form is best taken as a jussive of prayer, “may he answer us.” However, if the imperative in the previous line is emended to a perfect, the prefixed form is best taken as imperfect, “he will answer us” (see the note on the word “king” at the end of the previous line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the day we call.”
